beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output.
beats.got: Output alone won't tell you if an agent is safe, so you need a separate check.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: **Apply** named agent risk patterns (direct and indirect prompt injection, secrets in context, tool confusion, skill supply chain) and a plain access review
beats.got: There's a named list of agent risk patterns. I know most of them already.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I'm meant to list my checks before I see the tool's list.

beats.trigger: Ask the agent three questions in your own session. Ask which tools it can use right now.
beats.got: nothing new. I use tool calls daily.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: Nothing about agents is certain, and the lecture says so up front.

beats.trigger: That is why perimeter, access control and patching work.
beats.got: nothing new. Old software was deterministic.

beats.trigger: One passing test is one sample.
beats.got: One passing test proves very little for an agent. I've been treating a green run as proof.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (two agents, different trust levels). Filter (post-process output). Gate (human approves). Review (a second agent judges).
beats.got: Five mitigation moves with names. Handy for talking to my team.

beats.trigger: **"I can't tell"** is a real answer.
beats.got: Write down the leftover risk and sign for it. Sensible, but it's paperwork.

beats.trigger: Scope it down far enough and the system is safe and useless.
beats.got: Less access means less usefulness, and I have to pick the point. I would rather add capability.

beats.trigger: Should the agent read from that mailbox? If not, don't connect it.
beats.got: Not connecting a source is a mitigation. That gives me a question to ask before I wire up the sales team's mailbox.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: nothing new. It's a pep talk.

beats.trigger: a skill is a reusable check you run again instead of re-prompting from memory.
beats.got: A skill is a reusable check. I already use skills.

beats.trigger: Read the first few rows: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: Policy files run against my system and give a report with rows. Some rows need judgment.

beats.trigger: Push back on anything that sounds like a generic GDPR brochure.
beats.got: I tell it what actually matters here and it shapes the check around that. Faster than reading the policies.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: One skill, two lenses, built through a long interview. I'd rather it just build and I fix after.

beats.trigger: *"You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."*
beats.got: I can hand the decisions back with one line. I'll reuse it.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/agent-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: The skill gets installed into my skills folder.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: The skill is saved. It doesn't replace normal controls.

beats.trigger: The goal is the loop (assess, mitigate, reassess residual), not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: The aim is to run the loop once, not to pass.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: nothing new. Slash command loads the skill.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The audit found issues in my own system that I hadn't thought of. This is the first part that's new to me.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: A ranked risk list for my setup. Some of it I'd brushed off. I'm still going to build the thing.

beats.trigger: Your gut is data here.
beats.got: I pick the risk that bugs me and the agent applies a mitigation. The risk doesn't go away, I just write down what's left.

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can answer is sitting in the report.
beats.got: If I'm stuck I show the report to legal or security with a narrow question.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: One mitigation doesn't make it production. The rest of the list is still my job, and that applies to my engineers' agents too.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is the expert in the room, and it carries to the next agent.
beats.got: The check is reusable and the report holds the decisions.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the audit session and adds one to five rules to the root instructions file for future sessions.
beats.got: The session's findings turn into rules in the instructions file. Good, that's the carry-over.

beats.trigger: Their agent loads the same method by name without your prompt history.
beats.got: I can hand a teammate a skill and their agent runs the same method. Useful for rolling out to non-engineers.

beats.trigger: Well-formed English is the attack surface, even via sources.
beats.got: nothing new. Recap.

beats.trigger: Without the two sentences, you'll be writing them while the rest of the room is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: Homework. I probably won't do it.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two cases about fabricated or unchecked output. Skimming later maybe.

take_homes: Not connecting a source or removing a tool is the cheapest mitigation. Ask 'should it have this door at all' before I wire anything up.
The audit skill found things in my own system that I hadn't thought of. I'll run it on the other agents we have, and on whatever I build for sales.
One mitigation doesn't make an agent production-ready. I need to write down the residual risk and who signed for it.

monday.move: Run the agent-audit skill on one of our engineers' existing agents and read the risk report.
monday.who: me, then the engineer who owns that agent
monday.stop_condition: Stop when I have the ranked risk list and one residual decision written down.
monday.blocker: The engineer may not want an audit of their agent, and the skill's policy lens is built on my own policy dictation, not a real legal-reviewed policy.

misconception.why: The audit found things I hadn't considered and left others as 'I can't tell'. 'Good agent means good output' doesn't hold if the output can't tell me whether the agent is safe. I still think the checking steps in the first module were ceremony.

one_line: Good middle third, the door-you-don't-open idea and the audit are worth the time. The framing is slow if you already run agents.
